PROTECTED; clear.

PROTECTED; clear and faithful; 'deme of Cydathenaeum' reads as a place from context.
PROTECTED; clear and faithful.
Plain, faithful dialogue.
Plain dialogue line.
Clear; announces that Aristodemus's own words follow.

evidence: "he asked him where he was going, that he had turned himself into such a fine figure" — Victorian consecutive 'that'-clause plus a he/him/he/he pronoun chain; a listener loses who asked whom and why
paragraphs.fix: Light: a plain question from Aristodemus to Socrates about where he was going so dressed up, keeping the bath and the unusual sandals.

paragraphs.note: Clear; keeps the finery/fine-man wordplay.

evidence: "'I'll do as you bid me,' I replied." — the first first-person line of Aristodemus's account comes straight after 'He said that he met Socrates'; readers and listeners take 'I' for the narrator Apollodorus, who was not there (1.3, 1.5)
"bid me" — dated for 'tell me'
paragraphs.fix: Light: make it plain that Aristodemus is speaking (Plato marks this with a recurring 'he said'), in everyday wording.

paragraphs.note: Plain dialogue line.
Quoted proverb; verse word order is acceptable and clear in context.
Plain link line. The joke rests on Agathon's name meaning 'good'; Jowett leaves it implicit and the substitution still reads.
Quoted proverb; clear.

evidence: "not only demolishes but literally outrages the proverb" — 'outrage' in its old sense of 'violate'; today it reads as 'make angry'
"come unbidden to Agamemnon's banquet, the man who was feasting and offering sacrifices" — dangling apposition hung on a possessive
paragraphs.fix: Light: show in plain order that Homer goes further and reverses the proverb: the weak Menelaus arrives uninvited at the brave Agamemnon's sacrificial feast, the worse coming to the better.

paragraphs.note: Clear. Typography only: the stray closing quote and comma after 'who' should be tidied with 1.22 so the verse line completes his sentence.
Quoted verse line; clear in context.

evidence: "I was bidden of you" — archaic passive with 'of' (invited by you)
"But I shall say that I was bidden of you, and then you'll have to make an excuse for me." — Aristodemus's speech has lost its quotation marks, so 'you' reads as Apollodorus addressing his companion
paragraphs.fix: Light: everyday wording (he will say Socrates invited him, so Socrates must do the explaining) and restore Aristodemus's quotation marks consistently across 1.20–1.22.

paragraphs.note: Homeric half-line quotation; reads with 1.24.

evidence: "one or other of them may invent an excuse by the way" — 'by the way' now means 'incidentally'; here it means 'on the way'
paragraphs.fix: Light: 'on the way' or equivalent, keeping it recognisable as Socrates' playful Homeric tag.

evidence: "in a fit of abstraction" — dated for 'lost in thought'; readers now take 'abstraction' as abstract ideas
"You are just in time to sup with us" — archaic 'sup'
"put it off and make one of us" — archaic idiom for 'join us'
"meant to have asked you, if I could have found you" — Victorian perfect infinitive
paragraphs.fix: Light: everyday wording for Socrates lost in thought, joining the dinner and 'I meant to invite you', keeping every beat of the comic arrival without Socrates.

evidence: "I turned round, but Socrates was nowhere to be seen." — switches to Aristodemus as 'I' right after 1.25 calls him 'Aristodemus'/'he'; readers take 'I' for Apollodorus
paragraphs.fix: Light: signal that Aristodemus is the one telling this (a 'he told me'-type tag); the rest of the paragraph already reads well.

paragraphs.note: Plain dialogue line.
Plain dialogue line.
Plain dialogue; 'boy' as address to a servant is clear in context.

evidence: "'There he is fixed,'" — odd today ('fixed' = repaired); means rooted to the spot
"had retired into the portico of the neighboring house" — 'retired into' = withdrew into (now read as 'stopped working'/'went to bed')
"The servant then assisted him to wash, and he lay down." — stiff; 'lay down' means took his place on the dining couch
paragraphs.fix: Light: plain wording for washing, reclining at table, Socrates withdrawing into the neighbour's porch and standing motionless, deaf to the servant's calls.

paragraphs.note: Plain dialogue line.
Clear; 'do not therefore disturb him' is slightly stiff but plain in meaning, and 'my informant' was set up in 1.1.

evidence: "begged him to take the place next to him. ''I may touch you,' he said" — Jowett's purpose link ('that' = so that) is lost, so 'I may touch you' reads as an odd statement or request; doubled opening quotation marks
"until you had found what you sought.''" — doubled closing quotation marks
"for the fit, as usual, was not of long duration" — stiff; 'the fit' needs to read as his trance
paragraphs.fix: Light: restore the purpose link (sit by me so that I can touch you and share that wise thought), fix the doubled quotation marks and lighten the stiff narration, keeping Agathon's teasing.

evidence: "taking his place as he was desired" — 'desired' = asked
"as water runs through wool out of a fuller cup into an emptier one" — the wool-thread siphon needs a few words to be pictured
"how greatly should I value the privilege" — inverted
"a stream of wisdom plenteous and fair" — archaic 'plenteous', postposed adjectives
"of a very mean and questionable sort" — 'mean' = poor, shabby; now read as 'unkind'
"was manifested forth in all the splendor of youth" — archaic
paragraphs.fix: Substantive: present-day wording that keeps Socrates' irony and every image, makes the wool-thread siphon picturable, and replaces 'mean', 'plenteous' and 'manifested forth'.

evidence: "who bears off the palm of wisdom" — archaic idiom (wins the prize)
"of this Dionysus shall be the judge" — inverted; Dionysus (god of wine and of the drama festival Agathon has just won) named without context
"at present you are better occupied with supper" — stiff
paragraphs.fix: Light: everyday idiom for the coming wisdom contest, a few words placing Dionysus as god of wine and the theatre, and a plain 'for now, eat'.

evidence: "and supped with the rest" — archaic
"Then libations were offered" — drink-offerings poured for the gods; readers may take it as drinks being served
"I feel severely the effects of yesterday's potations" — archaic 'potations', inverted adverb
"for you were of the party yesterday" — dated
paragraphs.fix: Light: plain narration of the meal, the wine-offerings to the gods and the hymn, and Pausanias's hangover joke in everyday words.

paragraphs.note: Clear dialogue; 'drowned in drink' is vivid, not obscure.
Clear dialogue.
Plain dialogue line; 'not equal to it' is still current.

evidence: "the weak heads like myself" — dated idiom for low tolerance of wine; can be heard as 'weak-minded'
"others who never can drink" — inverted
"drinking deep is a bad practice" — dated
"yesterday's carouse" — archaic noun (also 'any one' here vs 'anyone' elsewhere)
paragraphs.fix: Light: modern idiom for holding one's drink and heavy drinking, keeping the aside about Socrates and Eryximachus's doctorly pomposity.

paragraphs.note: Clear; 'the Myrrhinusian' is a deme tag (optionally 'of Myrrhinus').
Plain narration.
Clear; the formal motion language ('I move...') suits Eryximachus's pomposity, and 'the women who are within' is understandable.

evidence: "after the manner of Melanippe in Euripides" — character and play named without context and 'after the manner of' is dated; readers cannot tell that a borrowed line is coming
paragraphs.fix: Light: signal that he is borrowing a line spoken by Melanippe in a play by Euripides, so 'Not mine the word' reads as 'these words are not mine'.

paragraphs.note: Quoted tragic half-line; clear once 1.44 flags the quotation.

evidence: "has no encomiast among all the poets who are so many" — rare word (writer of praise) and a clumsy relative
"the excellent Prodicus, for example, who have descanted in prose on the virtues of Heracles" — archaic 'descanted'; sophists and Prodicus unexplained; 'Prodicus ... who have' does not agree
"many other like things have had a like honor bestowed upon them" — stiff
"And only to think that there should have been such eager interest created about them" — Victorian exclamation
"no one has ever dared worthily to hymn Love's praises! So entirely has this great deity been neglected." — archaic and inverted
"For often he says to me in an indignant tone: What a strange thing it is" — Phaedrus's quoted complaint has no quotation marks, so its end (before 'Now in this Phaedrus...') is unmarked
paragraphs.fix: Substantive: present-day English keeping every item (hymns to other gods, sophists like Prodicus praising Heracles in prose, the book praising salt), mark where Phaedrus's complaint ends, and keep the left-to-right speech proposal.

evidence: "How can I oppose your motion, who profess to understand nothing but matters of love?" — 'who' hangs after 'your motion' and must be traced back to 'I'
"there can be no doubt of Aristophanes, whose whole concern is with Dionysus and Aphrodite" — needs a few words: a comic poet, whose gods stand for wine/theatre and love
"Nor will anyone disagree of those whom I see around me." — ungrammatical today
"desired him to do as Socrates bade him" — archaic
paragraphs.fix: Substantive: present-day syntax for Socrates' support of the motion, keeping his claim to know only about love, a few words glossing Aristophanes' Dionysus-and-Aphrodite joke, and a plain closing line.

paragraphs.note: Plain narration; clear by eye and ear.

evidence: "a proof of his claim to this honor is that of his parents there is no memorial" — inverted clause; 'memorial' = record; by ear 'that of his parents' misparses
paragraphs.fix: Light: say plainly that the proof is that no poet or prose writer records his parents (optionally 'the poet Hesiod').

paragraphs.note: Quoted Hesiod verse; clear.

evidence: "Parmenides also sings of Generation:" — Parmenides named without context; 'sings of Generation' (a personified power of coming-into-being) is opaque, and the 'he' of the next verse has no clear subject
paragraphs.fix: Light: a few words identifying Parmenides as a philosopher-poet and Generation as the power that 'fashioned Love' in his poem, leaving Jowett's verse wording intact.

paragraphs.note: Quoted verse; fine once 2.2 says who 'he' (Generation) is; 'train' = procession, poetic but readable.

evidence: "Thus numerous are the witnesses who acknowledge Love to be the eldest of the gods." — inverted

"For the principle which ought to guide men who would live nobly — that principle, I say, neither kindred, nor honor, nor wealth, nor any other motive is able to implant so well as love." — object-fronted periodic sentence; 'kindred' = family
"a virtuous lover, or to the lover than a beloved youth" — the Greek convention (an older male lover, a younger male beloved) that the whole speech rests on is never made plain
"some way of contriving that a state or an army should be made up of lovers and their loves" — dated 'contriving'; 'lovers and their loves' is confusing
"emulating one another in honor" — 'emulate' here = compete
paragraphs.fix: Substantive: natural modern sentences; establish in a few words the older-lover/younger-beloved roles (and who Acusilaus is); keep the shame-before-the-beloved argument and the army-of-lovers image in order.

evidence: "what lover would not choose rather to be seen by all mankind than by his beloved" — dated 'choose rather'
"The veriest coward would become an inspired hero" — archaic 'veriest'
"That courage which, as Homer says, the god breathes into the souls of some heroes, Love of his own nature infuses into the lover." — object-fronted; 'of his own nature' obscure
paragraphs.fix: Substantive: modern word order and vocabulary for the lover's shame at deserting or throwing away his arms, the coward turned hero, and Love giving the lover by nature the courage Homer's god breathes into heroes.

evidence: "Of this, Alcestis, the daughter of Pelias, is a monument to all Greece" — inverted opening
"among the many who have done virtuously" — archaic
"such exceeding honor is paid by the gods" — archaic 'exceeding'
"But Orpheus, the son of Oeagrus, the harper, they sent empty away" — object-fronted; archaic 'empty away'
"presented him only with an apparition of her whom he sought" — archaic; readers need to know he had gone down to Hades for his dead wife
paragraphs.fix: Substantive: plain narration of both myths in sequence (Alcestis dies for her husband and is sent back; Orpheus seeks his dead wife in Hades, gets only a phantom, later dies at women's hands), keeping all Jowett's judgments.

evidence: "the true love of Achilles toward his lover Patroclus — his lover and not his love" — turns on the lover/beloved roles; 'his lover and not his love' is opaque
"a foolish error into which Aeschylus has fallen" — Aeschylus (the tragedian who made Achilles the lover in a play) named without context
"And greatly as the gods honor the virtue of love, still the return of love on the part of the beloved to the lover is more admired" — concessive inversion
"because he is inspired by God" — capital-G 'God' reads as the monotheistic God; the sense is possessed by a god
"if he abstained from slaying Hector" — archaic; readers need to know Hector had killed Patroclus
"not only in his defense, but even after he was dead" — unclear whose death (Patroclus's)
paragraphs.fix: Substantive: state plainly that Patroclus was the older lover and Achilles the younger beloved (so Achilles' sacrifice ranks higher), identify Aeschylus and Hector's killing of Patroclus in a few words, use 'a god', and keep the closing summary.

paragraphs.note: Already modern, clear and faithful. Typography: Pausanias's speech (3.0–3.9) has no quotation marks while chapter 1 and 4 speech does; harmonize book-wide. Optional: '(the Sky)' after Uranus would show why she is 'heavenly'.
Modern and clear; the two-Loves argument is easy to follow. Optional: 'meaner' (= baser) and 'wantonness' are slightly dated.
Modern and clear. Only soft spot: 'play the fool with them' here means make fools of them.
PROTECTED; clear, no genuine defect. Optional glosses: Lacedaemon = Sparta; 'the barbarians' = non-Greek (Persian) rule.
Modern, clear and faithful.
Modern and clear; 'forswear himself' is explained by the lover's-oath clause.

evidence: "Evil is the vulgar lover" — 'vulgar' here means of the Common (popular) Aphrodite, not crude; the link to 3.0–3.1 is lost
"it encourages some to pursue and others to flee" — never says that lovers pursue and the beloved flee
"the love of a noble disposition lasts a lifetime" — ambiguous; means the lover of a noble character
paragraphs.fix: Light: tie 'vulgar' to the Common love of 3.1, make clear that custom urges lovers to pursue and the beloved to hold off so the contest shows which kind each is, and say it is the lover of a noble character who stays for life.

paragraphs.note: PROTECTED; clear and faithful.
PROTECTED; clear. Jowett's quoted 'uses base' is a literary allusion that still reads in context.
Modern, clear and faithful.

evidence: "Eryximachus, he said, you ought either to cure my hiccups or speak in my turn until they stop." — no quotation marks, so 'Eryximachus, he said' reads as 'Eryximachus said'; the speaker is Aristophanes

"Pausanias came to a pause — this is the balanced way of speaking I've been taught by the wise." — Apollodorus is mocking the rhetoricians' name-jingles (Pausanias/pause); a modern reader will miss the joke
paragraphs.fix: Light: quote and name Aristophanes as speaker, and let the aside read clearly as a joke about the jingling style that fashionable speech-teachers taught.

paragraphs.note: Modern and clear. Typography only: add quotation marks for Eryximachus's and Aristophanes' lines, as in chapter 1.

evidence: "my art informs me further that this double love is not merely an affection of the human soul toward the fair" — 'my art' (his craft, medicine), 'affection' (state) and 'the fair' (the beautiful) are all old senses
"that I may do honor to my art" — archaic purpose clause
"which are confessedly different and unlike, and being unlike, they have loves and desires which are unlike" — archaic 'confessedly'; circular stacked clauses
"to indulge good men is honorable and bad men dishonorable" — 'indulge' = gratify (Pausanias's sense of yielding to a lover); elliptical
"but discouraged.'" — closing quotation mark here although the speech runs on to 4.5
paragraphs.fix: Substantive: present-day sentences that keep Eryximachus's systematic, slightly pompous tone and every step (the double love reaches beyond the soul to all bodies and nature; healthy vs diseased desire), make 'indulge' clear, and keep the speech's quotation open until 4.5.

evidence: "in this the art of medicine consists" — inverted
"able to separate fair love from foul" — archaic 'fair/foul'
"My ancestor Asclepius" — needs a few words: the legendary founder of medicine, from whom doctors claimed descent
"as the poets here tell us" — 'here' = the poets at this table (Agathon, Aristophanes)
"the arts of gymnastics and husbandry, are under his dominion" — archaic 'husbandry' (farming); 'his' reads as Asclepius, but the speech's claim is Love's rule
"for he says that The One is united by disunion, like the harmony of the bow and the lyre" — Heraclitus's riddle needs a few words (the opposing tension that holds a bow or lyre together)
paragraphs.fix: Substantive: plain modern wording with brief context for Asclepius and Heraclitus's bow-and-lyre image, and a clear referent for 'his dominion' (the god Love, whose 'empire' 4.0 describes), keeping the hot/cold, bitter/sweet pairs.

evidence: "For harmony is a symphony, and symphony is an agreement" — 'symphony' now means an orchestral work; here it means concord, sounding together
"but an agreement of disagreements while they disagree there cannot be" — inverted
"which accordance, as in the former instance medicine, so in all these other cases music implants" — Victorian relative with ellipsis; a listener cannot follow it
"there is no difficulty in discerning love which has not yet become double" — the point (in pure theory there is no good/bad split; it appears in practice) is not made plain

"the correct performance of airs or metres already composed (which latter is called education)" — archaic 'airs'; British 'metres' against the edition's American spelling; why performing is 'education' needs a few words
paragraphs.fix: Substantive: rebuild the reconciliation-of-opposites argument in plain steps (high/low notes, long/short beats, music implanting love as medicine does), replace 'symphony', and make the theory-versus-practice point and 'education' clear.

evidence: "the love of Urania the fair and heavenly muse" — needs a few words: Urania ('Heavenly') is the Muse matching the Heavenly Love of 3.0
"the vulgar Polyhymnia" — 'vulgar' = common, popular (the Common Love), not crude; Polyhymnia ('many hymns') unexplained
"the duty of accepting the temperate, and those who are as yet intemperate only that they may become temperate" — 'accepting' = gratifying; the purpose clause is lost by ear
"who must be used with circumspection" — formal
"it is a great matter so to regulate the desires of the epicure" — archaic
"both loves ought to be noted as far as may be" — archaic
paragraphs.fix: Substantive: explain the two Muses as the musical counterparts of Heavenly and Common love, unpack who is to be gratified and why, and put the gourmet analogy and the conclusion into present-day English.

evidence: "which to know in relation to the revolutions of the heavenly bodies and the seasons of the year is termed astronomy" — fronted relative with an infinitive subject; 'astronomy' here covers weather and seasons
"But the wanton love, getting the upper hand" — dated 'wanton' (unruly, excessive)
"the whole province of divination, which is the art of communion between gods and men" — archaic 'province'; divination (reading signs from the gods) needs its sense clear
"all manner of impiety is likely to ensue" — formal
"Wherefore the business of divination is to see to these loves" — archaic
paragraphs.fix: Substantive: plain sentences for the seasons (balanced love brings health and plenty, unruly love plague, frost and blight), for what 'astronomy' studies, and for divination tending and healing the two loves between gods and men.

evidence: "And the love, more especially, which is concerned with the good, and which is perfected in the company of temperance and justice, whether among gods or men, has the greatest power" — stacked relatives delay the verb
"I dare say that I too have omitted several things" — dated
"take some other line of commendation" — archaic
"I perceive that you are rid of the hiccough" — stiff; 'hiccough' is the old spelling (chapter 3 has 'hiccups') and risks a 'hic-cough' reading in audio
paragraphs.fix: Light: bring the verb forward in the first sentence and put the hand-over to Aristophanes into everyday words, keeping Eryximachus's formal politeness; spell 'hiccups' as in chapter 3.

evidence: "the hiccough is gone" — old spelling; chapter 3 has 'hiccups'
"said Aristophanes, who followed" — means 'who was next to speak'
"not, however, until I applied the sneezing" — keep the mock-medical 'applied', but 'the sneeze' is idiomatic
paragraphs.fix: Light: spelling and idiom only, keeping Aristophanes' parody of Eryximachus's medical jargon about the body's 'harmony'.

evidence: "Beware, friend Aristophanes" — dated address
"although you are going to speak, you are making fun of me" — 'although' obscures the point (you are joking just before your own speech)

"I shall have to watch and see whether I cannot have a laugh at your expense, when you might speak in peace" — near double negative; the threat to watch his speech for anything laughable, when he could have spoken unmolested, is lost
paragraphs.fix: Substantive: make Eryximachus's warning plain: because Aristophanes jokes before his speech, Eryximachus will watch it for something to laugh at, when he could have spoken in peace.

evidence: "I will unsay my words" — archaic (I take it back)
"which is to the manner born of our muse" — Shakespearean idiom; 'our muse' = comedy, Aristophanes' art
paragraphs.fix: Substantive: plain wording that keeps the joke's distinction: being laughed with is natural to a comic poet and welcome; being laughed at as ridiculous is what he fears.

paragraphs.note: Clear enough: 'shoot your bolt and escape' reads literally (take your shot and get away). Optional: tag Eryximachus as speaker for listeners.
